Title: High‐Performing Nanofiber Memristor via Field‐Induced Ion Migration Concentration at Highly‐Curved Interwoven Interface
Text:
RESEARCH ARTICLE
www.small-journal.com
High-Performing Nanoﬁber Memristor via Field-Induced Ion
Migration Concentration at Highly-Curved Interwoven
Interface
Yue Liu, Yuanhang Zhang, Xufeng Zhou, Zhuming Wang, Zhe Yang, Jialin Meng,
Chen Wang, Xuemei Sun, Lin Chen,* Peining Chen,* and Huisheng Peng
Memristors with high computing capabilities hold signiﬁcant potential as
processing devices in the era of information explosion, but their applications
are largely hindered by the trade-oﬀbetween memristive performance and
operation uniformity. Extensive eﬀorts are devoted to designing or regulating
memristive layers of memristors to improve device performance, while few
studies focused on the interface structure at cross points of memristors.
Herein, inspired by the tip eﬀect, a nanoﬁber memristor with highly-curved
interwoven interface is designed by assembling nanoﬁber electrodes using
dielectrophoretic method. The nanoﬁber memristor shows high operation
uniformity with an ultralow set voltage standard deviation of 0.014 V, which is
even superior to that of state-of-the-art oxide-based planar memristors.
Experimental and simulation analysis reveals that the highly-curved interface
can eﬃciently concentrate electric ﬁeld distribution and conﬁne the switching
region, thus facilitating the migration of silver ions and suppressing the
formation of random conductive ﬁlaments. Nanoﬁber memristor arrays with
good device reproducibility are further integrated for fundamental logic gate
circuits like NOT, AND, and OR. This work oﬀers a new insight for
constructing high-performing nanoelectronics.

1. Introduction
Emerging technologies such as the Inter-
net of Things and artiﬁcial intelligence have
driven the explosive growth of intricate data,
which calls for changes in information pro-
cessors to meet energy-eﬃcient and area-
eﬃcient computing demands.[1] Memris-
tor crossbars capable of in-suit information
storing and processing are considered to be
the most promising circuit-building blocks
to address the challenge of the big data
era.[2] Each memristor unit in the crossbar
array is composed of two electrodes sand-
wiching a memristive layer, and the resis-
tive switching process is realized by the
reversible formation and rupture of con-
ductive ﬁlaments in the memristive layer.[3]
However, the growth pathways of conduc-
tive ﬁlaments are generally random at the
working interface, thus leading to unavoid-
able temporal and spatial variations in de-
vice performance.[4] Therefore, achieving
a high-performing memristor with desired
operation uniformity is urgently needed for
the practical application of memristors.
For traditional planar memristors with nearly uniform elec-
trical distribution between the electrode, their variable oper-
ating performance generally originates from the random ion
transportation and conductive ﬁlament growth in the homoge-
neous memristive layer.[5] To this end, extensive eﬀorts have
been explored to enhance operation uniformity by designing het-
erogeneous memristive layers, such as doping conductive im-
purities, introducing grain boundaries and designing aligned
nanochannels.[6] Using heterogeneous memristive layers can
promote operation uniformity of memristors, but to some de-
gree, it may sacriﬁce the memristive performance like operating
voltage.[7] It remains challenging to realize high memristive per-
formance and operation uniformity just by regulating the com-
position and/or structure of memristive materials.
As is well known, tip eﬀect is a common physical eﬀect re-
ferring to energy concentration occurring at the tip region with
high curvature, which can induce local enhancement of elec-
tric, magnetic or thermal ﬁelds.[8] Speciﬁcally, compared with
planar counterparts, the electric ﬁeld can be greatly enhanced
at the curved tip due to the concentration of electrons for an

electriﬁed tip, and such ﬁeld enhancement is intensiﬁed with the
increase of curvature. That is, the energy at tip interface could be
precisely controlled and transferred through the tip eﬀect, which
has been widely used in the ﬁelds of catalysis, energy conversion
and water capture.[9] Previous memristors have been mostly stud-
ied based on a paradigm of planar structure, in which the electric
ﬁeld is uniformly distributed at the interface between planar elec-
trodes. Recently, memristors based on ﬁber structure have been
constructed from micro to macro scale,[10] providing a promis-
ing clue to develop high-performance memristors through ratio-
nal structural design. We hypothesize if the tip eﬀect is intro-
duced into the memristor by designing highly-curved crossbar
electrodes, the electric ﬁeld distribution would be concentrated at
the tip interface to precisely conﬁne the ion transport and growth
of conductive ﬁlament. The resultant memristors are poised to re-
alize both low operating voltage and good operation uniformity.
Herein, we present such a memristor with a highly-curved in-
terface by preparing Pt and SiO2/Ag ﬁbers at the nanoscale as
memristive electrodes. The nanoﬁber electrodes were selected
because of the smaller diameter oﬀers higher curvature. The
nanoﬁber electrodes were interlaced with each other to form a
memristor unit through dielectrophoretic assembling method
(Figure 1a). The nanoﬁbers were prepared by electrochemical de-
position method with the assistance of porous rigid templates.
The resultant memristor exhibited an ultralow voltage standard
deviation of 0.014 V under a low set voltage of 0.18 V, which
is superior to state-of-the-art planar memristors made of metal
oxide memristive materials (Figure 1b,c). Such high operation
uniformity and low set voltage mainly originated from the lo-
cal electric ﬁeld enhancement and conﬁned growth of conduc-
tive ﬁlament at the interwoven interface between nanoﬁber elec-
trodes. As a proof-of-concept, memristor arrays with good de-
vice reproducibility were further achieved by interweaving multi-
ple nanoﬁber electrodes, and demonstrated basic logic gate func-
tions including NOT, AND, and OR.
2. Results and Discussion
Nanoﬁbers as the building blocks of memristors were fabricated
through electrochemical deposition method (Figure S1, Support-
ing Information).[11] An anodic aluminum oxide (AAO) mem-
brane with aligned nanopores and controllable size was selected
as the assisted template to prepare high-quality nanoﬁbers.[12]
Under the applied electric ﬁeld, the AAO template in the three-
electrode compartmented electrochemical cell served as cathode
to drive metal ions toward nanopores in the electrolyte. These
metal ions formed crystal nuclei in the nanopores after electro-
chemical reactions. After metal atoms ﬁlled in the nanopores,
Ag and Pt nanoﬁbers were obtained by dissolving AAO mem-
brane using alkaline solution (Figure S2, Supporting Informa-
tion). Beneﬁting from the conﬁnement eﬀect of nanopores in
the AAO membrane, the fabricated nanoﬁbers exhibited a high

aspect ratio (length/diameter), with a length of ≈20–30 μm and a
diameter of ≈300 nm (Figure S3, Supporting Information). Such
high aspect ratio could eﬃciently promote aligned arrangement
during the following assembly process. As shown in Figure S3
(Supporting Information), the surface of the whole nanoﬁber was
smooth and uniform, ensuring the interwoven electrodes were
closely contact with each other. Moreover, the nanoﬁber showed
a typical single-crystal structure, which could promote carrier
transportation and improve device performance (Figure S4, Sup-
porting Information).[13]
Dielectrophoretic assembly is recognized as the promising
bottom-up fabrication approach for precisely and ﬂexibly ma-
nipulating various nanoﬁbers to fabricate nanodevices.[14] In a
typical dielectrophoretic assembly process (Figure S5, Support-
ing Information), a microchip patterned with plenty of parallel
electrode pairs was mounted into a ﬂuid cell, and then the dis-
persion liquid containing nanoﬁbers ﬂowed across its surface
with a constant ﬂow rate. When an external voltage was applied
to electrode pairs on the microchip, these nanoﬁbers in disper-
sion were polarized by the charge separation at their surface
due to the positive Clausius–Mossetti factor.[15] The dipolar mo-
ment along the nanoﬁber exhibited a sluggish response to the
alternating and nonuniform electric ﬁeld, thus generating pos-
itive dielectrophoretic force toward the electrode tips with high
charge density.[16] Then, the polarized nanoﬁbers were driven
along the gradient of the electric ﬁeld and assembled at the neigh-
boring electrode pair (Figure S6, Supporting Information). Ac-
cording to the simulating result of the assembly system (Figure
S7, Supporting Information), the nanoﬁbers are subjected to di-
electrophoretic force toward the electrode tips along the electric
ﬁeld gradient, which increases with the rise of amplitude and fre-
quency of applied alternating current.[15,17] Subsequently, the as-
sembled nanoﬁbers were further adhered and welded onto the
electrode pairs by applying a higher voltage to form van der Waals
connection. By precisely controlling the applied voltage and ﬂow
rate during the dielectrophoretic assembly process, nanoﬁbers
were assembled and aligned at the desired position (Figure S8,
Supporting Information). The surface structure of nanoﬁbers
was well maintained after assembly process (Figure 1d,e).
After assembling the bottom electrode of the nanoﬁber mem-
ristor, silicon dioxide (SiO2) with a thickness of 10 nm and amor-
phous structure was deposited as the memristive layer through
electronic beam evaporation (Figure S9, Supporting Informa-
tion), which exhibited high structural defect density for opti-
mal memristive performances.[18] The SiO2 was used as mem-
ristive layer due to its simple composition, modulation conve-
nience, scalability and compatibility with the complementary
metal-oxide semiconductor technology. Then, the top electrode
of the nanoﬁber memristor was assembled at the vertical elec-
trode pair to interlace with the bottom nanoﬁber electrode de-
posited with SiO2 (Figure S10, Supporting Information). Finally,
a nanoﬁber memristor unit consisting of Pt and Ag nanoﬁber
electrodes was constructed (Figures S11 and S12, Supporting In-
formation), which can be easily extended to various materials and
fabricated at large scale compared with the reported nanoscale
crossbar memristor.[10a]
The resistive switching behavior of the nanoﬁber mem-
ristor unit was investigated by applying a direct voltage to
the Ag nanoﬁber electrode, while grounding the Pt nanoﬁber
electrode (Figure 2a). During the direct current sweeps, the
nanoﬁber memristor exhibited a typical non-volatile bipolar re-
sistive switching behavior (Figures 2b and S13, Supporting Infor-
mation). The operating voltage of nanoﬁber memristor showed
a low set voltage of 0.18 V, and it was stably maintained in the
investigated 30 switching cycles, which were superior to those of
the reported nanoscale memristors.[10a] Moreover, the nanoﬁber
memristor showed a high on-oﬀratio (>105) and good endurance
stability even after 1000 switching cycles at an elevated tempera-
ture (Figures 2c and S14, Supporting Information), which is ben-
eﬁcial to alleviate the crosstalk issue in the nanoﬁber memristor
crossbar array.[2a,19] The resistance of low resistance state (LRS)
could be readily tuned from 102 to 105 Ω by changing the com-
pliance current, which endowed the memristor with multiple re-
sistance states to achieve multi-level memory (Figure S15, Sup-
porting Information). And the resistances of diﬀerent resistance
state for the nanoﬁber memristor were stably maintained dur-
ing an operating duration of 1000 s (Figure 2d), indicating its
retention reliability. In addition, both the high resistance state
(HRS) and LRS remained stable even after an extended retention
of 10 000 s under a high temperature of 85 °C (Figure S16, Sup-
porting Information). For the performance of diﬀerent devices,
30 nanoﬁber memristors were analyzed and all of them exhib-
ited typical resistive switching behaviors with a slight set voltage
variation of 10% (Figure S17, Supporting Information), indicat-
ing their excellent device-to-device reproducibility. Overall, the
nanoﬁber memristors demonstrated good comprehensive elec-
trical performances, including a low average set voltage of 0.18
V with a slight standard deviation of 0.014 V (Figure 2e). To our
best knowledge, compared with the state-of-the-art oxide-based
memristors,[20] the nanoﬁber memristor achieved the lowest set
voltage and voltage standard deviation (Figure 2f).
The resistive switching mechanism of nanoﬁber memristors
was carefully studied. As shown in Figure 3a, when a set voltage is
applied, Ag ions are generated at the surface of the Ag nanoﬁber
electrode by anodic dissolution, and then migrate through the
SiO2 memristive layer with the help of the external electric ﬁeld.
Due to the tip eﬀect at the high-curvature nanoﬁbers (Figure 3b),
the electric ﬁeld in the memristive layer is locally enhanced and
concentrated at the interlaced point, thus eﬀectively facilitating
the transportation of Ag ions toward the Pt nanoﬁber electrode.
Then, the migrated Ag ions are continually reduced to Ag atoms
at the surface of the Pt nanoﬁber electrode, and the reduced Ag
atoms gradually accumulate to form a conductive silver ﬁlament.
The growth of conductive silver ﬁlament is orderly and eﬀectively
conﬁned at the nanoscale interlacing area. As a result, the unique
interface structure of the nanoﬁber memristor contributes to lo-
cal electric ﬁeld enhancement and forms a contact point that is
comparable to the size of a single conductive ﬁlament, thus en-
dowing the memristor with ultralow set voltage and high opera-
tion uniformity.
To further study the inﬂuence of interface structure on the
device performances, memristors with diﬀerent interface struc-
tures were fabricated for systematic comparisons (Figure 3).
First, the memristor with a traditional planar-to-planar structure
was fabricated by interlacing Pt and Ag planar electrodes (with a
width of 300 nm) through the top-down processes (Figure 3c,d).
Second, the memristor with a nanoﬁber-to-planar structure was
fabricated by replacing the Ag planar electrode with an Ag

nanoﬁber electrode (with a diameter of 300 nm) through the hy-

memristor with a nanoﬁber-to-nanoﬁber structure was created
by substituting both Pt and Ag electrodes in the memristor of

eter of 300 nm) (Figure 3i,j). The memristive layer in the above
three types of memristor is shared with the same SiO2 with a
thickness of 10 nm.
To study the resistive switching properties of these memris-
tors with diﬀerent interface structures, the Ag top electrode as
working electrode was connected with the semiconductor char-
acterization system to supply external voltage, while the Pt bot-
tom electrode as counter electrode was grounded. For the mem-
ristor made from planar Pt and Ag electrodes, its current-voltage
curves exhibited a typical non-volatile bipolar resistive switching
behavior with an average set voltage of 0.458 V, combined with a
voltage standard deviation of 0.216 V in the 30 cycles of switch-
ing (Figures S18a and S19a,b, Supporting Information), and the
HRS and LRS resistance showed obvious ﬂuctuation under direct
current sweeps. As shown in Figures S18b and S19c,d, Support-
ing Information, the memristor made from planar Pt electrode
and Ag nanoﬁber electrode demonstrated a similar non-volatile
bipolar resistive switching behavior, which had a lower set voltage
(0.233 V) and voltage standard deviation (0.088 V) than that made
from planar Pt and Ag electrodes. Moreover, it showed higher en-
durance stability than that made from planar Pt and Ag electrodes
under repeated switching cycles.
By comparing the memristive performance of memristors
with diﬀerent structures, the set voltage variation of the mem-
ristor made from nanoﬁber Pt and Ag electrodes was the low-
est among the three types of memristors, indicating its good
operation uniformity during the consecutive operating process
(Figure 3l,m). In addition, the resistance values of HRS for the
memristor made from interlaced Pt and Ag nanoﬁber electrodes
were also well maintained during the 30 switching cycles, com-
pared with the larger ﬂuctuations of those for the other two types
of memristors (Figure S20, Supporting Information). That is be-
cause the resistive switching behavior of ﬁlament-based mem-
ristors greatly depends on the migration of metal ions and the
growth of conductive ﬁlament in the memristive layer. We fur-
ther performed ﬁnite element simulation to compare the elec-
tric ﬁeld distribution at the interlacing interface. As shown in
Figures 3e,h,k and S21, Supporting Information, the electric ﬁeld
at the interlacing area for nanoﬁber memristors and nanoﬁber-
to-planar memristors were mainly distributed at the contact in-
terface, which can promote the formation of conductive ﬁla-
ment. However, the electric ﬁeld distribution of planar memris-
tors mainly focused on the sharp edge of electrodes, which might
cause weaker spots and poor reliability.[21] In addition, the size of
contact region for nanoﬁber memristors was smaller, which was
almost comparable to that of a single conductive ﬁlament. Such
small contact region could eﬀectively suppress the formation
of random conductive ﬁlaments, thus endowing the nanoﬁber
memristors with superior operation uniformity.

By using the dielectrophoretic assembly approach, the ba-
sic logic gates were formed to realize complex functions,
including NOT gate, AND gate and OR gate.[23] For the NOT
gate, a nanoﬁber memristor was conﬁgured at a low resistance
state and connected with a constant resistor (Figure 4c). In this
circuit, a high voltage (or current) was deﬁned as a logic 1, while
a low voltage (or current) as a logic 0. If the voltage of input A
was low (logic 0), then this logic operation generated a high out-
put current of A’ (logic 1); if a high input voltage of A (logic 1)
was applied, the current of output A’ was switched to low (logic
0, Figure 4f). Furthermore, an AND gate was fabricated by con-
necting two nanoﬁber memristors in parallel and followed with
a constant resistor in series (Figure 4d). In this circuit, the low
current of output C (logic 0) was observed with either one or
two low input voltages (logic 0), and the output current was high
(logic 1) only when both the inputs A and B were high (logic 1,
Figure 4g). As another logic operation, OR gate was obtained with
two nanoﬁber memristors and a ﬁxed load resistor connected in
series (Figure 4e). The logic 0 was performed with low current of
output C, when both input A and B were low voltages (logic 0).
But if either of the inputs was high voltage (logic 1), the output C
in this structure was high (logic 1, Figure 4h). Overall, realizing
the above basic logic gates by assembling nanoﬁber memristors
represented the possibility of implementing functional logic cir-
cuits and complex computation.
3. Conclusion
In summary, nanoﬁber memristors made from interlaced
nanoﬁber electrodes were prepared using dielectrophoretic as-
sembly method. The nanoﬁber memristor exhibited a low set
voltage (0.18 V) with an ultralow standard deviation of set voltage
(0.014 V). Such superior operation uniformity was attributed to
the unique highly-curved interface between the nanoﬁber elec-
trodes, which could induce local enhancement of electric ﬁeld
and conﬁne the growth of conductive ﬁlaments. Furthermore,
the nanoﬁber memristor arrays with good device-to-device re-
producibility were fabricated to realize typical logic-gate func-
tions, conceptually verifying the feasibility of a nanoscale storing
and computing chip based on the scalable bottom-top assembly
approach.
4. Experimental Section
Materials:
Anodic aluminum oxide (AAO) membrane was purchased
from Shenzhen Topmembranes Technology (Anodic, with a diameter of
25 mm, pore diameter of 300 nm, thickness of 40 μm). Hexachloropla-
tinic Acid Hexahydrate (H2PtCl6⋅6H2O, Pt 37.5%), potassium phosphate
monobasic (KH2PO4, 99.5%) and potassium phosphate dibasic anhy-
drous (K2HPO4, 99%) were purchased from Aladdin. Orthoboric acid
(H3BO3, 99.5%), silver sulfate (Ag2SO4, 99.99%) and potassium thio-
cyanate (KSCN, 99%) were purchased from Macklin Inc. Nitric acid so-
lution (HNO3, 90%) and sodium hydroxide monohydrate (NaOH, 98%)
were obtained from Sigma Aldrich. These materials were used as received
without further treatment.
The Synthesis of Nanoﬁber:
Pt and Ag nanoﬁbers were synthesized by
electrochemical deposition with a porous AAO membrane as template in a
three-electrode compartmented electrochemical cell. First, one side of the
AAO template was sputtered with a thin Au ﬁlm (with a thickness of 50
nm) to serve as working electrode. Then, the electrochemical deposition
process was conducted by the CHI 760D electrochemical workstation with
a KCl-saturated Ag/AgCl electrode as reference electrode and an inert Pt
plate as counter electrode. The Pt nanoﬁbers were grown by direct current
electrodeposition at a constant current density of 0.5 mA cm−2 and de-
position time of 12 h in an aqueous electrolyte containing H2PtCl6⋅6H2O
(10 g L−1) and H3BO3 (12 g L−1). For the growth of Ag nanoﬁbers, the elec-
trolyte was composed of Ag2SO4 (16 g L−1), KSCN (224 g L−1), KH2PO4
(12 g L−1) and K2HPO4 (50 g L−1). After growth completion, the AAO
template was taken out from the electrochemical cell and rinsed several
times with deionized water. Subsequently, nanoﬁbers were released from
the porous template by etching the bottom Au ﬁlm with HNO3 (378 g L−1)
aqueous solution and dissolving the AAO template using NaOH (120
g L−1) aqueous solution. Finally, the prepared nanoﬁbers were suﬃciently
rinsed with deionized water and then dispersed in isopropyl alcohol sol-
vent under soniﬁcation.
The Assembly of Nanoﬁbers:
The nanoﬁbers were assembled by the di-
electrophoretic assembly method in ﬂuid cell. First, a microﬂuidic chip
with patterned and aligned electrodes was fabricated on the SiO2/Si wafer
substrates by photolithography, magnetron sputtering deposition and lift-
oﬀtechniques. The structure of each electrode was composed of 10 nm
Ti as adhesion layer and 100 nm Pt (or Ag) as conducting layer. Then, the
microﬂuidic chip was mounted into a sealed ﬂuid cell with micropipes to
provide nanoﬁber suspension and a transparent quartz window to moni-
tor the assembly process. Simultaneously, electrode pairs on the chip were
connected with a resistor of 1 KΩ to limit current and a waveform func-
tion generator (Model 645, Berkeley Nucleonics Corp., USA) to operate the
assembly process. As the nanoﬁbers steadily ﬂowed through the ﬂuid cell
with a constant ﬂow rate of 1 mL min−1, they became trapped by electrode
pairs on the surface of the microﬂuidic chip under alternating voltage at
a frequency range of 1 kHz and a root-mean-square voltage of 1 V. Finally,
the ordered and stable nanoﬁbers were obtained by ﬂushing the excess
nanoﬁbers with isopropyl alcohol solvent and locking the contact points
with higher applied voltage.
The Fabrication of Memristors with Diﬀerent Structures:
Nanoﬁber
memristors composed of interlaced Pt and Ag nanoﬁber electrodes were
fabricated by nanoﬁber dielectrophoretic assembly and memristive mate-
rial deposition processes. After the electrode pairs were prepared with 10
nm Ti and 100 nm Pt, Pt nanoﬁbers were assembled on the microﬂuidic
chip as bottom electrodes. Then, SiO2 with a thickness of 10 nm was de-
posited as a memristive layer by electronic beam evaporation technique.
Finally, Ag nanoﬁbers were assembled as top electrodes onto the perpen-
dicular patterned electrode pairs consisting of 10 nm Ti and 400 nm Ag,
thus interlacing with the above Pt nanoﬁbers to form nanoﬁber memris-
tors. For memristors made from interwoven Pt planar and Ag nanoﬁber
electrodes, the bottom planar electrodes with a width of 300 nm were fab-
ricated by electron beam photolithography, magnetron sputtering deposi-
tion and lift-oﬀtechniques, while the preparation of the memristive layer
and top nanoﬁber electrodes were similar to that of nanoﬁber memris-
tors. For memristors made from interwoven Pt and Ag planar electrodes,
both bottom and top planar electrodes with a width of 300 nm were all
fabricated by electron beam photolithography, magnetron sputtering de-
position and lift-oﬀtechniques, while the preparation of memristive layer
was the same as that of nanoﬁber memristors.
The Preparation of Nanoﬁber Memristor-based Logic Gate Circuit:
The
NOT logic gate circuit was composed of one nanoﬁber memristor with
Ag nanoﬁber as the A input terminal and Pt nanoﬁber as the A’ out-
put terminal. In the case of AND logic gate circuit, a nanoﬁber memris-
tor was ﬁrst fabricated with Ag bottom nanoﬁber as the A input termi-
nal. Then, another nanoﬁber memristor was directly assembled above it
with Ag nanoﬁber as the B input terminal and Pt nanoﬁber as the C out-
put terminal. For the construction of OR logic gate circuit, two nanoﬁber
memristors were assembled with two paralleled Ag nanoﬁbers as the
A and B input terminals and one shared Pt nanoﬁber as the C output
terminal.
Characterization:
The morphologies of nanoﬁbers and nanoﬁber
memristors were characterized through ﬁeld emission scanning electron
microscopy (SEM, Zeiss Gemini SEM500 FESEM operated at 5 kV; EDS,
Aztec X-Max Extreme EDS operated at 10 kV), transmission electron mi-

Finite Element Simulation:
The distribution of electric ﬁeld and dielec-
trophoretic force were simulated using ﬁnite element analysis. To study
the dielectrophoretic assembly process, a two-dimensional model was de-
veloped, consisting of a pair of electrodes and nanoﬁber suspension. The
electrode pair was set with a thickness of 100 nm and a gap of 20 μm
and applied with an external voltage of 1 V. The nanoﬁber suspension
ﬂowed along the positive direction of the X-axis with a constant ﬂow rate
of 0.1 m s−1. To study the memristors with diﬀerent structures, a three-
dimensional model was developed, consisting of memristive layer, bot-
tom and top electrodes. For the memristor made from interlaced Ag and
Pt planar electrodes, the planar electrodes were set with a width of 300 nm
and a thickness of 100 nm, and the SiO2 memristive layer was set with a
thickness of 10 nm. For the memristor made from interlaced Ag nanoﬁber
and Pt planar electrodes, the bottom electrode and memristive layer were
similar to those of the memristor made from interlaced Ag and Pt pla-
nar electrodes, while the top electrode was replaced as nanoﬁber with a
diameter of 300 nm. For the memristor made from interlaced Ag and Pt
nanoﬁber electrodes, the diameter of nanoﬁber electrodes was set as 300
nm and the thickness of SiO2 memristive ﬁlm was set as 10 nm. All of the
interlaced electrodes were applied with an external voltage of 0.2 V. The
material properties of electrodes, nanoﬁber suspension and memristive
ﬁlm were set up according to the Materials Library in the software. Free
tetrahedral meshing was used for the electrodes, suspension and mem-
ristive domains.
Statistical Analysis:
The set voltage variation is deﬁned as the standard
deviation of set voltage divided by its average value.
